title: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax

hero.subtitle: The universal syntax for identifying resources on the Internet

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) provides a simple and extensible means for identifying a resource. This specification defines the generic URI syntax and the process for resolving URI references.

URIs are the foundation of the Web. Every URL you type in a browser, every API endpoint, and every resource link follows this specification. Understanding URI syntax is essential for web development and Internet protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a standard way to name a resource, such as a web page. This RFC defines the generic URI syntax and how to resolve a URI reference. Every URL typed in a browser, every API endpoint and every resource link follows it.

sections.title: Characters
sections.content:
URIs are composed of a limited set of characters. Characters outside this set must be percent-encoded.

UnreservedA-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~
Reserved (gen-delims): / ? # [ ] @
Reserved (sub-delims)! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =
Percent-Encoding Examples
Space       -> %20
Forward /   -> %2F (in path segments)
Question ?  -> %3F (in path)
Ampersand & -> %26 (in query values)
UTF-8 char  -> %E2%9C%93 (checkmark)
sections.plainLanguage: URIs use a limited set of characters: letters, digits and a few symbols, plus reserved characters such as / ? # [ ] @ that have special roles. Any other character must be percent-encoded, written as % and two hex digits. A space becomes %20.

sections.title: Syntax Components
sections.content:
The generic URI syntax consists of a hierarchical sequence of five components:

URI Component Breakdown
         foo://example.com:8042/over/there?name=ferret#nose
         \_/   \______________/\_________/ \_________/ \__/
          |           |            |            |        |
       scheme     authority       path        query   fragment
schemeIdentifies the protocol (http, https, ftp, mailto, etc.)Required
authority[userinfo@]host[:port] - identifies the serverOptional
pathHierarchical path to the resourceRequired (may be empty)
queryNon-hierarchical key-value parametersOptional
fragmentSecondary resource identifier (client-side only)Optional
sections.plainLanguage: A URI has up to five components: scheme, authority, path, query and fragment. The scheme (such as http) is required. The authority names the server, optionally with user information and a port. The path is required but may be empty. The query and fragment are optional.

sections.title: Reference Resolution
sections.content:
Relative references allow URIs to be expressed relative to a base URI. The resolution algorithm transforms a relative reference into its target URI.

Reference Resolution Examples
Base URI: http://a/b/c/d;p?q

"g:h"       -> g:h            (different scheme)
"g"         -> http://a/b/c/g  (relative path)
"./g"       -> http://a/b/c/g  (same as above)
"../g"      -> http://a/b/g    (parent directory)
"//g"       -> http://g        (network-path)
"?y"        -> http://a/b/c/d;p?y  (query override)
"#s"        -> http://a/b/c/d;p?q#s (fragment only)

Relative references are heavily used in HTML (links, images, stylesheets) and HTTP (Location header redirects). The resolution algorithm must handle edge cases like empty paths, double dots, and scheme-relative references.
sections.plainLanguage: A relative reference is a URI written relative to a base URI. The resolution algorithm turns it into a full target URI. For example, with base http://a/b/c/d;p?q, the reference ../g resolves to http://a/b/g. HTML links and HTTP redirects use this heavily.

sections.title: Normalization
sections.content:
URI normalization converts URIs into a canonical form, enabling comparison of URIs that may be syntactically different but semantically equivalent.

Case Normalization
Scheme and host are case-insensitive and should be lowercased. Percent-encoding hex digits should be uppercased (e.g., %2f -> %2F).
Percent-Encoding Normalization
Unreserved characters that are percent-encoded should be decoded (e.g., %41 -> A).
Path Segment Normalization
Dot segments (. and ..) in the path should be resolved and removed.
Port Normalization
Default ports should be removed (e.g., http://example.com:80/ -> http://example.com/).
sections.plainLanguage: Normalization converts URIs to a standard form so that equivalent ones can be compared. It lowercases the scheme and host, uppercases percent-encoding hex digits, decodes percent-encoded unreserved characters, removes dot segments from the path, and drops default ports.

sections.title: URI, URL, and URN
sections.content:
The terms URI, URL, and URN are often confused. This specification clarifies their relationship.

Term
Description
Example
URI
Generic identifier for any resource
Any URL or URN
URL
URI that provides location/access mechanism
https://example.com/page
URN
URI that provides persistent name
urn:isbn:0451450523

In practice, the terms URI and URL are often used interchangeably. The distinction matters primarily in formal specifications. All URLs are URIs, and all URNs are URIs, but not all URIs are URLs or URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: A URI is a generic identifier for any resource. A URL is a URI that says where and how to reach the resource. A URN is a URI that gives a persistent name. All URLs and URNs are URIs, but not every URI is either, and in practice URI and URL are often used interchangeably.

subtitle: The universal syntax for identifying resources on the Internet.

tldr.problem: Every program had its own way of writing down where something lives, so a link written in one tool could mean nothing in another.
tldr.mechanism: One grammar, scheme:[//authority]path[?query][#fragment], with a fixed set of reserved delimiters, percent-encoding for everything else, and an exact algorithm for turning a relative reference into a full URI.
tldr.outcome: Web links, API endpoints and mailto: addresses all follow it. It replaced RFC 2396 and is still the generic syntax today (STD 66).

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3986 defines the generic syntax of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs), the strings that name resources on the Web. It specifies the allowed characters, the five components, how relative references are resolved against a base, and how to normalize URIs for comparison.

questions: what is the difference between a uri and a url
what characters are allowed in a url
how do i normalize a url for comparison
today: Browsers do not implement this RFC to the letter: they follow the WHATWG URL Standard, which parses malformed input more leniently and is the reference for what new URL() does in JavaScript. RFC 3986 remains the generic grammar that protocol specifications and HTTP libraries point to. Non-ASCII addresses are handled by Internationalized Resource Identifiers (RFC 3987), which map back onto the percent-encoded form defined here.

implementations.name: WHATWG URL Standard
implementations.note: The living spec browsers implement; close to, but not identical to, RFC 3986.
